    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1211.1351v1</id>
    <title>Visible Points in Convex Sets and Best Approximation</title>
    <updated>2012-11-06T19:14:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.1351v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1211.1351v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The concept of a visible point of a convex set relative to a given point is introduced. A number of basic properties of such visible point sets is developed. In particular, it is shown that this concept is useful in the study of best approximation, and it also seems to have potential value in the study of robotics.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00022v3</id>
    <title>A note on visible islands</title>
    <updated>2022-02-14T16:44:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00022v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2109.00022v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Given a finite point set $P$ in the plane, a subset $S \subseteq P$ is called an island in $P$ if $conv(S) \cap P = S$. We say that $S\subset P$ is a visible island if the points in $S$ are pairwise visible and $S$ is an island in $P$. The famous Big-line Big-clique Conjecture states that for any $k \geq 3$ and $\ell \geq 4$, there is an integer $n = n(k,\ell)$, such that every finite set of at least $n$ points in the plane contains $\ell$ collinear points or $k$ pairwise visible points. In this paper, we show that this conjecture is false for visible islands, by replacing each point in a Horton set by a triple of collinear points. Hence, there are arbitrarily large finite point sets in the plane with no 4 collinear members and no visible island of size $13$.</summary>
    <category term="math.CO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1209.3594v5</id>
    <title>On Universal Point Sets for Planar Graphs</title>
    <updated>2013-08-27T13:20:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.3594v5" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1209.3594v5" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A set P of points in R^2 is n-universal, if every planar graph on n vertices admits a plane straight-line embedding on P. Answering a question by Kobourov, we show that there is no n-universal point set of size n, for any n>=15. Conversely, we use a computer program to show that there exist universal point sets for all n<=10 and to enumerate all corresponding order types. Finally, we describe a collection G of 7'393 planar graphs on 35 vertices that do not admit a simultaneous geometric embedding without mapping, that is, no set of 35 points in the plane supports a plane straight-line embedding of all graphs in G.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08066v2</id>
    <title>Edge complexity of geometric graphs on convex independent point sets</title>
    <updated>2017-04-21T10:13:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.08066v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1605.08066v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we focus on a generalised version of Gabriel graphs known as Locally Gabriel graphs ($LGGs$) and Unit distance graphs ($UDGs$) on convexly independent point sets. $UDGs$ are sub graphs of $LGGs$. We give a simpler proof for the claim that $LGGs$ on convex independent point sets have $2n \log n + O(n)$ edges. Then we prove that unit distance graphs on convex independent point sets have $O(n)$ edges improving the previous known bound of $O(n \log n)$.</summary>
